title: Single Human-AI Fit: One Attribute, Seven Channels, Two Directions
description:
A system built for an average user charges everyone else for the difference. We ask whether that charge is measurable in language models, where the deviation is one fact a person states about themselves.

We run a counterfactual audit on three open models. One detail changes; everything else stays byte-identical. Seven methods read seven channels, from trait attribution and task accuracy to forced choice and self-report.

Four behavioural channels agree that disclosure costs the person. A fifth, the one closest to what a conventional audit measures, moves the other way: asked for a numeric score, all three models rate the person higher, and that holds against two different neutral references. The divergence is specific to the two disability disclosures; age moves every channel down.

Negative results are reported: a model cannot say where a disclosure changed its answer, stability does not degrade, and one method failed.

A reversal between rating and ranking has been reported before. What we add is the unit of analysis, one person read through seven interactions, and the consequence: an audit still sees a difference, but the channel decides which way it points. All data and code are public, and every number regenerates without a GPU.
